title: Adam is every man
source_text: Ἐπὰν δὲ φάσκῃ ὡς ἄρα ἀνοσιώτατα τὸν θεὸν, εὐθὺς καὶ ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς ἀσθενοῦντα καὶ μηδ᾿ ἕνα ἄνθρωπον, ὃν αὐτὸς ἔπλασε. πεῖσαι δυνάμενον. εἰσήγαγεν ὁ Μωϋσέως λόγος, καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο φήσομεν ὅτι ὅμοιόν ἐστι τὸ λεγόμενον, ὡς εἴ τις ἐνεκάλει ἐπὶ τῇ τῆς κακίας συστάσει, ἣν οὐδὲ ἀπὸ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου δεδύνηται κωλῦσαι ὁ θεὸς, ὥστε κἂν ἕνα τινὰ ἄνθρωπον εὑρεθῆναι ἀρχῆθεν ἄγευστον κακίας γεγενημένον. ὡς γὰρ περὶ τούτου οἷς μέλει ἀπολογεῖσθαι περὶ προνοίας ἀπολογοῦνται οὐ δι᾿ ὀλίγων οὐδὲ δι᾿ εὐκαταφρονήτων, οὕτω δὲ καὶ περὶ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ καὶ περὶ τῆς ἁμαρτίας αὐτοῦ φιλοσοφήσουσιν οἱ ἐγνωκότες ὅτι καθ᾿ Ἑλλάδα φωνὴν ὁ Ἀδὰμ ἄνθρωπός ἐστι, καὶ ἐν τοῖς δοκοῦσι περὶ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ εἶναι φυσιολογεῖ Μωϋσῆς τὰ περὶ τῆς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου φύσεως. καὶ „γὰρ ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ,“ ὥς φησιν ὁ λόγος, „πάντες ἀποθνῄσκουσι,“ καὶ κατεδικάσθησαν ἐν „τῷ ὁμοιώματι τῆς παραβάσεως Ἀδὰμ,“ οὐχ οὕτως περὶ ἑνός τινος ὡς περὶ ὅλου τοῦ γένους ταῦτα φάσκοντος τοῦ θείου λόγου. καὶ γὰρ ἐν τῇ τῶν λεγομένων ὡς περὶ ἑνὸς ἀκολουθίᾳ ἡ ἀρὰ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ κοινὴ πάντων ἐστί· καὶ τὰ κατὰ τῆς γυναικὸς οὐκ ἔστι καθ᾿ ἧς οὐ λέγεται. καὶ ὁ ἐκβαλλόμενος δὲ ἐκ τοῦ παραδείσου ἄνθρωπος μετὰ τῆς γυναικὸς, τοὺς „δερματίνους“ ἠμφιεσμένος „χιτῶνας,“ οὓς διὰ τὴν παράβασιν τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐποίησε τοῖς ἁμαρτήσασιν ὁ θεὸς, ἀπόῤῥητόν τινα καὶ μυστικὸν ἔχει λόγον, ὑπὲρ τὴν κατὰ Πλάτωνα κάθ (οδ) ον τῆς ψυχῆς, πτεροῤῥυούσης καὶ δεῦρο φερομένης, „ἕως ἂν στερεοῦ τινος λάβηται.“
pass_a_gloss: When he asserts (φάσκω) that most impiously (ἀνοσίως, superl.) the account (λόγος) of Moses introduced (εἰσάγω) God being weak (ἀσθενέω) straight away (εὐθύς) and from the beginning (ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς) and not able to persuade (πείθω) even one man whom he himself formed (πλάσσω), to this too we will say that what is said is similar, as if someone were to accuse (ἐγκαλέω) at the existence/constitution (σύστασις) of wickedness (κακία), which God has not been able to prevent (κωλύω) even from one man, so that at least (κἄν) one man be found from the beginning (ἀρχῆθεν) born untasting (ἄγευστος) of wickedness. For as about this those to whom it is a care (μέλει) to defend (ἀπολογέομαι) concerning providence (πρόνοια) defend not through few nor through contemptible (εὐκαταφρόνητος) [arguments], so also about Adam and about his sin (ἁμαρτία) those will philosophize (φιλοσοφέω) who have known that according to the Greek tongue (Ἑλλὰς φωνή) Adam is 'man' (ἄνθρωπος), and in the things seeming to be about Adam Moses treats physically / gives an account of nature (φυσιολογέω) of the things about the nature (φύσις) of man. For also 'in Adam,' as the word says, 'all die' (ἀποθνῄσκω), and they were condemned (καταδικάζω) in 'the likeness (ὁμοίωμα) of Adam's transgression (παράβασις),' the divine word asserting these things not so much about some one as about the whole race (γένος). For also in the sequence (ἀκολουθία) of the things said as about one, the curse (ἀρά) of Adam is common (κοινός) to all; and the things against the woman, there is not [a woman] against whom they are not said. And the man being cast out (ἐκβάλλω) from the paradise with the woman, clothed (ἀμφιέννυμι) in the 'garments of skin' (δερμάτινοι χιτῶνες) which on account of the transgression of men God made for those who sinned, has a certain secret (ἀπόρρητος) and mystical (μυστικός) meaning (λόγος), above (ὑπέρ) the descent (κάθοδος) of the soul according to Plato, shedding its wings (πτερορρυέω) and being carried (φέρω) hither 'until it takes hold of (λαμβάνομαι) something solid (στερεός).'
pass_b_english: When he says that “the story of Moses most impiously brings in God as weak straight away, from the very beginning, and unable to persuade even one man whom he himself had formed,” to this too we shall say that the charge is like a complaint against the existence of wickedness, which God has not been able to prevent even in a single man, so that at least one man might be found who from the beginning had never tasted wickedness. For just as those who care to defend providence make their defence on this point with arguments neither few nor contemptible, so too those will philosophize about Adam and his sin who know that the name Adam, in Greek, is “man,” and that in what seems to be about Adam, Moses is giving an account of the nature of man.

For “in Adam,” as the word says, “all die” (1 Corinthians 15:22), and they were condemned “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Romans 5:14), the divine word saying these things not so much of one particular man as of the whole race. Indeed, in the sequence of what is said as though of one man, the curse of Adam is common to all (Genesis 3:17–19); and as for what is said against the woman, there is no woman of whom it is not said (Genesis 3:16). And the man who is cast out of paradise with the woman (Genesis 3:23–24), clothed in the “garments of skins” (Genesis 3:21) which, because of the transgression of humankind, God made for those who had sinned, holds a secret and mystical meaning, beyond the descent of the soul as Plato tells it, which sheds its wings and is carried down here “until it lays hold of something solid” (Plato, Phaedrus 246c).

choices.choice: τὸν θεόν … εἰσήγαγεν: 'brings in a God who is weak' -> 'brings in God as weak' (article kept, Celsus names Israel's God)
ἄγευστον κακίας γεγενημένον: 'had been born without any taste of' -> 'had never tasted' (removed 'born')
διὰ τὴν παράβασιν moved next to ἐποίησε so it modifies God's making of the garments, not 'those who had sinned'
κατὰ Πλάτωνα κάθοδον: 'Plato's descent of the soul' -> 'the descent of the soul as Plato tells it'
checked 1 Corinthians 15:22, Romans 5:14, Genesis 3:16, 3:17-19, 3:21, 3:23-24, Plato, Phaedrus 246c: all correct

Celsus's charge is introduced by 'φάσκῃ ὡς ἄρα …' (reported speech with Celsus's own wording and Origen's ironic ἄρα); it is put in quotation marks as Celsus's words, with 'he says that' kept as the frame. 'τῇ τῆς κακίας συστάσει' rendered 'the existence of wickedness'. 'καθ᾿ Ἑλλάδα φωνὴν ὁ Ἀδὰμ ἄνθρωπός ἐστι': Origen means that the Hebrew name Adam, put into Greek, is ἄνθρωπος ('man', human being). φυσιολογεῖ rendered 'is giving an account of the nature of'. 1 Corinthians 15:22 quoted exactly (ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ πάντες ἀποθνῄσκουσιν). Romans 5:14 is adapted: Paul speaks of those who did not sin 'ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι τῆς παραβάσεως Ἀδάμ'; Origen applies the phrase (with ἐν) to all who were condemned; translated as Origen has it. 'The curse of Adam' alludes to Genesis 3:17–19 and 'what is said against the woman' to Genesis 3:16; expulsion Genesis 3:23–24; 'χιτῶνας δερματίνους' Genesis 3:21 LXX. Plato citation certain: Phaedrus 246c (ἡ δὲ πτερορρυήσασα φέρεται ἕως ἂν στερεοῦ τινος ἀντιλάβηται); Origen has λάβηται. κάθ(οδ)ον is Koetschau's restoration, accepted. Origen's own view of the 'garments of skins' is left as he leaves it here, a 'secret and mystical meaning', with nothing added. ἀρχῆθεν ἄγευστον κακίας γεγενημένον rendered 'who from the beginning had never tasted wickedness' (γεγενημένον is 'having been', not 'born').
